t: Checking Existence of Edge Length Limited Paths II — Online Bottleneck Connectivity
o:
Each query asks: if we delete every edge of distance ≥ limit, are p and q still connected? Equivalently, among all p–q paths, does the one minimizing the heaviest edge (the bottleneck path) have weight strictly below limit?
Example 1: query(2,3,2) is true because the single edge 2–3 of distance 1 suffices; query(1,3,3) is false because reaching node 1 already costs 2 and every continuation onto 3 costs at least 1 more with nothing cheaper available; query(2,0,3) is true via 2 → 3 → 0 with weights 1 and 2; query(0,5,6) is false because components {0,1,2,3} and {4,5} never touch.
The classic offline trick (sort queries by limit, sweep edges into a union-find — LC 1697) fails here because queries arrive online, interleaved in arbitrary order. The repair is to move all sorting to the edge side: run Kruskal once in increasing distance order and freeze snapshots of that process so any threshold can be answered later in logarithmic time. Both approaches below do exactly this. Constraints (n, |E|, #queries ≤ 10^4, distances up to 10^9) fit comfortably in an O((E + N) log + Q log N) budget.
k: Connectivity under a weight cap is monotone in the cap, so it equals connectivity in the minimum spanning forest built up to that cap.
The path minimizing the maximum edge weight between two nodes always lies in the minimum spanning forest (the minimax/bottleneck property).
Online queries rule out sort-by-limit DSU sweeps; binary lifting over a merge history restores O(log n) answers.

a.n: Approach 1: Minimum Spanning Forest Plus Max-Edge Binary Lifting
a.i: Run Kruskal on edges sorted by distance and keep only the accepted tree edges; by the bottleneck property, p and q are connected under cap limit exactly when they lie in the same MSF tree and the heaviest edge on their tree path is < limit. Root each tree, then build binary-lifting tables storing, for every 2^k jump, both the ancestor and the maximum edge weight along it (−1 marks "beyond the root"). A query levels the two nodes while accumulating maxima, then lifts them toward their LCA — never stepping past a root — and compares the accumulated bottleneck with limit; failing to meet means disconnected.
s: Sort edges by distance and run Kruskal, appending accepted edges to an adjacency list.
Root each tree with an iterative DFS recording parent, edge-to-parent weight, and depth.
Build tables up[k][v] (2^k-th ancestor or −1) and heavy[k][v] (max edge weight on that jump).

Query: raise the deeper node accumulating maxima, lift both nodes together only through defined ancestors, accumulate the last step, and answer max-so-far < limit (any −1 at the meeting point → disconnected).
a.t: Build O(E log E + N log N) — Kruskal sort plus lifting tables; each query O(log N).
a.sp: O(N log N) for the lifting tables plus O(N + E) adjacency.

a.i: Replay Kruskal but never merge into an existing root: every successful union creates a brand-new internal node whose two children are the old roots and whose stored weight is the edge distance; original vertices become leaves (allocate 2n − 1 node slots, filling ids from n upward). By construction weights increase toward the root, two vertices become connected precisely when their lowest common ancestor is created, and that LCA’s weight is exactly their bottleneck distance. So each query reduces to one LCA lookup over plain parent pointers — no max-tracking table needed.
s: Sort edges ascending; initialize parent pointers over 2n slots with leaves 0..n−1 first.
For each edge whose endpoints sit in different trees, create internal node id (starting at n) with weight = distance and set it as parent of both old roots.
Build binary lifting over these parents; compute depths by scanning ids downward (a parent is always created after its children, hence has a larger index).
Query: level the two nodes, descend together; if their final parents differ they are disconnected, otherwise answer weight[LCA] < limit.
a.t: Same asymptotics as Approach 1 — O(E log E + N log N) build, O(log N) per query — with smaller constants since no edge-weight table is maintained.
a.sp: O(N log N) for the ancestor table over at most 2N − 1 tree nodes.

w: Start from the offline DSU solution of LC 1697, explain why interleaved online queries break it, then offer either structure — Approach 2 is less code and less state, Approach 1 connects directly to familiar LCA-on-MST reasoning. Pitfalls: strict inequality (answer with < limit, never <=); forests with several components (make cross-component queries return false rather than reading sentinel weights — treat "ancestor = none" explicitly); parallel edges (Kruskal naturally skips redundant ones). The constraints promise p != q, but short-circuiting p == q to true costs nothing and guards against surprises. Follow-ups: handle dynamic edge insertions (link-cut trees or Holm–de Lichtenberg–Thorup), report the actual bottleneck value instead of a boolean, or support edge deletions.
